verses.zh: 全能者既定期罚恶，为何不使认识他的人看见那日子呢？
verses.en: “Why are times not appointed by[NOTE:1] the Almighty?[NOTE:2] Why do those who know him not see his days?
notes: The preposition מִן (min) is used to express the cause (see GKC 389 §121.f).

The LXX reads “Why are times hidden from the Almighty?” as if to say that God is not interested in the events on the earth. The MT reading is saying that God fails to set the times for judgment and vindication and makes good sense as it stands.
verses.commentary:
24:1 "Why. . ." The NEB
removes the Hebrew term "why." This seems to put Job 24 in
line with 23:14. There are three cycles of speeches by the three
comforters of Job and his response to them. However, in the third cycle,
Zophar's speech is missing. Many commentators believe that Job 24 is not
the words of Job but the words of Zophar. If not the whole chapter, some
believe that at least Job 24:18-21 contain words from Zophar (cf.
Jerusalem Bible is one example of this).

▣ "the Almighty"
See
SPECIAL TOPIC: SHADDAI.

▣ "And why do those who know Him not see his days" Job is
asking why God doesn't have regular court days to deal with evil people. The ancient
belief was that God would have to set things straight in his life (i.e., "the two
ways"). When that is not the case, the afterlife becomes a necessity for the moral
justice of God (cf. Psalm 63), but this concept is not part of Job's theology.

The Hebrew word "know" (see

SPECIAL TOPIC: KNOW) has several connotations but here it refers to
innocent, righteous followers of God who know Him and His ways.

verses.zh: 有人挪移地界，抢夺群畜而牧养。
verses.en: Men[NOTE:1] move boundary stones;they seize the flock and pasture them.[NOTE:2]
notes: The line is short: “they move boundary stones.” So some commentators have supplied a subject, such as “wicked men.” The reason for its being wicked men is that to move the boundary stone was to encroach dishonestly on the lands of others (Deut 19:14; 27:17).

The LXX reads “and their shepherd.” Many commentators accept this reading. But the MT says that they graze the flocks that they have stolen. The difficulty with the MT reading is that there is no suffix on the final verb—but that is not an insurmountable difference.
verses.commentary:
24:2-12 This is a series of
violent crimes against the poor that God has not dealt with. Job

verses.zh: 他们拉去孤儿的驴，强取寡妇的牛为当头。
verses.en: They drive away the orphan’s donkey;they take the widow’s ox as a pledge.
verses.commentary:
24:3 "donkey. . .ox"
These are imagery for possessions in general. The wicked take everything
from the powerless and weak of society.

verses.zh: 他们使穷人离开正道；世上的贫民尽都隐藏。
verses.en: They turn the needy from the pathway,and the poor of the land hide themselves together.[NOTE:1]
notes: Because of the violence and oppression of the wicked, the poor and needy, the widows and orphans, all are deprived of their rights and forced out of the ways and into hiding just to survive.
verses.commentary:
24:4 "They pushed the needy aside from the road" This is a
Hebrew idiom (cf. Amos 2:7). The poor and powerless are robbed of their
rights as citizens. No justice for them!

24:4b "made to hide themselves"
The figures of speech are difficult to understand, but Job 24:4b-8,10-11
describes the plight of the displaced poor who are seeking food,
shelter, and warmth.

24:6b

NASB, NKJV, NRSV, JPSOA
"glean"

TEV, Peshitta
"gather"

NJB
"pilfering"

REB
"filch"

Moffatt
"rob"

This is a rare word (BDB 545, KB 536), which may mean "to despoil"
or "to gather late growth." The poor and powerless have been
driven from their land and homes. Now they must find their meager food
wherever they can.

The LXX translates this verse as "They reaped a field not their own
before its time."

verses.zh: 这些贫穷人如同野驴出到旷野，殷勤寻找食物；他们靠着野地给儿女糊口，
verses.en: Like[NOTE:1] wild donkeys in the wilderness,they[NOTE:2] go out to their labor[NOTE:3] seeking diligently for food;the arid rift valley[NOTE:4] provides[NOTE:5] food for them and for their children.
notes: The verse begins with הֵן (hen), but the LXX, Vulgate, and Syriac all have “like.” R. Gordis (Job, 265) takes הֵן (hen) as a pronoun “they” and supplies the comparative. The sense of the verse is clear in either case.
That is, “the poor.”

The MT has “in the working/labor of them,” or “when they labor.” Some commentators simply omit these words. Dhorme retains them and moves them to go with עֲרָבָה (ʿaravah), which he takes to mean “evening”; this gives a clause, “although they work until the evening.” Then, with many others, he takes לוֹ (lo) to be a negative and finishes the verse with “no food for the children.” Others make fewer changes in the text, and as a result do not come out with such a hopeless picture—there is some food found. The point is that they spend their time foraging for food, and they find just enough to survive, but it is a day-long activity. For Job, this shows how unrighteous the administration of the world actually is.

The rift valley (עֲרָבָה, ʿaravah) extends from Galilee to the Gulf of Aqaba, but the term normally refers only to a section of it. For the book of Job, the most likely section is that south of the Dead Sea, a section that is arid with only sparse vegetation.tc Based on the text critical question in the previous note, some read this as a form related to the noun עֶרֶב (ʿerev, “evening”). These same consonants occur as a verb in Isa 24:11, עָרְבָה (ʿarevah) from עָרַב (ʿarav, “become evening”). This would give the time frame of their work rather than the location, but the location provides a parallel to “wilderness.”
The verb is not included in the Hebrew text but is supplied in the translation.

verses.zh: 收割别人田间的禾稼，摘取恶人余剩的葡萄，
verses.en: They reap fodder[NOTE:1] in the fieldand glean[NOTE:2] in the vineyard of the wicked.
notes: The word בְּלִילוֹ (belilo) means “his fodder.” It is unclear to what this refers. If the suffix is taken as a collective, then it can be translated “they gather/reap their fodder.” The early versions all have “they reap in a field which is not his” (taking it as בְּלִי לוֹ, beli lo). A conjectural emendation would change the word to בַּלַּיְלָה (ballaylah, “in the night”). But there is no reason for this.

The verbs in this verse are uncertain. In the first line “reap” is used, and that would be the work of a hired man (and certainly not done at night). The meaning of this second verb is uncertain; it has been taken to mean “glean,” which would be the task of the poor.

verses.zh: 终夜赤身无衣，天气寒冷毫无遮盖，
verses.en: They spend the night naked because they lack clothing;they have no covering against the cold.
verses.commentary:
24:7 This is powerful imagery. It is not meant to denote a total
"nakedness" but ill equipped clothing.

verses.zh: 在山上被大雨淋湿，因没有避身之处就挨近磐石。
verses.en: They are soaked by mountain rainsand huddle[NOTE:1] in the rocks because they lack shelter.
notes: Heb “embrace” or “hug.”

verses.zh: 又有人从母怀中抢夺孤儿，强取穷人的衣服为当头，
verses.en: The fatherless child is snatched[NOTE:1] from the breast;[NOTE:2] the infant of the poor is taken as a pledge.[NOTE:3]
notes: The verb with no expressed subject is here again taken in the passive: “they snatch” becomes “[child] is snatched.”
This word is usually defined as “violence; ruin.” But elsewhere it does mean “breast” (Isa 60:16; 66:11), and that is certainly what it means here.

The MT has a very brief and strange reading: “they take as a pledge upon the poor.” This could be taken as “they take a pledge against the poor” (ESV). Kamphausen suggested that instead of עַל (ʿal, “against”) one should read עוּל (ʿul, “suckling”). This is supported by the parallelism. “They take as pledge” is also made passive here.
verses.commentary:
24:9 This verse seems to be out
of place. RSV puts it in parenthesis.

verses.zh: 使人赤身无衣，到处流行，且因饥饿扛抬禾捆，
verses.en: They go about naked, without clothing,and go hungry while they carry the sheaves.[NOTE:1]
notes: The point should not be missed—amidst abundant harvests, carrying sheaves about, they are still going hungry.

verses.zh: 在那些人的围墙内造油，榨酒，自己还口渴。
verses.en: They press out the olive oil between the rows of olive trees;[NOTE:1] they tread the winepresses while they are thirsty.[NOTE:2]
notes: The Hebrew term is שׁוּרֹתָם (shurotam), which may be translated “terraces” or “olive rows.” But that would not be the proper place to have a press to press the olives and make oil. E. Dhorme (Job, 360-61) proposes on the analogy of an Arabic word that this should be read as “millstones” (which he would also write in the dual). But the argument does not come from a clean cognate, but from a possible development of words. The meaning of “olive rows” works well enough.
The final verb, a preterite with the ו (vav) consecutive, is here interpreted as a circumstantial clause.
verses.commentary:
24:11

NASB
"within the walls"

NKJV
"within their walls"

NRSV
"between their terraces"

NJB
"two little walls"

JPSOA
"between rows (of olive trees)"

REB
"where two walls meet"

The term (BDB 1004) is an Arabic root (found only here and possibly in
Jer. 5:10) which is best translated something like JPSOA. This is the
suggestion of the UBS Text Project (p. 76). The poor work hard for
others but are themselves hungry and thirsty. This is the continuing
exploitation of the poor and powerless!

▣ "they produce oil"
This VERB (BDB 844, KB 1008, Hiphil
IMPERFECT) has two possible origins.

- to press out oil

- from a NOUN for "midday" or "noon"

The NJB translates it as "their shelter at high noon," but
most English translations relate it to "winepress."

verses.zh: 在多民的城内有人唉哼，受伤的人哀号；　神却不理会那恶人的愚妄。
verses.en: From the city the dying[NOTE:1] groan,and the wounded[NOTE:2] cry out for help,but God charges no one with wrongdoing.[NOTE:3]
notes: The MT as pointed reads “from the city of men they groan.” Most commentators change one vowel in מְתִים (metim) to get מֵתִים (metim) to get the active participle, “the dying.” This certainly fits the parallelism better, although sense could be made out of the MT.
Heb “the souls of the wounded,” which here refers to the wounded themselves.

The MT has the noun תִּפְלָה (tiflah) which means “folly; tastelessness” (cf. 1:22). The verb, which normally means “to place; to put,” would then be rendered “to impute; to charge.” This is certainly a workable translation in the context. Many commentators have emended the text, changing the noun to תְּפִלָּה (tefillah, “prayer”), and so then also the verb יָשִׂים (yasim, here “charges”) to יִשְׁמַע (yishmaʿ, “hears”). It reads: “But God does not hear the prayer”—referring to the groans.
verses.commentary:
24:12 "the souls of the wounded cry out" This is the Hebrew
term nephesh (BDB 659), which denotes a person. The poor cry out
as a person wounded in battle!

SPECIAL TOPIC: NEPHESH

▣ "Yet God does not pay attention to folly" This is the
key thought of Job's argument, that a just God is simply not paying attention
to His business (cf. Job 9:13-24; Ps. 73:2-14; Mal. 3:15)! There is no justice! How
can "the two ways" be the only explanation of God's ways with humans?

verses.zh: 又有人背弃光明，不认识光明的道，不住在光明的路上。
verses.en: There are those[NOTE:1] who rebel against the light;they do not know its ways, and they do not stay on its paths.
notes: Heb “They are among those who.”
verses.commentary:
24:13-19 contains another list of violent crimes that God has not dealt
with. Job wants to know where the justice of God is. Why does He not
regularly hold court?

Here is a list of the violations of God's ways
related to the poor and powerless in society.

- steal land by changing the boundary stones, Job 24:2a (cf. Deut. 19:14;
27:17; Pro. 22:28; 23:10)

- steal livestock, Job 24:2b (specific examples in 24:3b)

- steal the donkeys of orphans

- steal the oxen from widows (cf. Exod. 22:22; Deut. 24:17)

- exploit the poor, Job 24:4-8,10-11

- drive them out

- steal their crops

- cause them to beg

- make them homeless and in need

- steal the children as slaves for money due, Job 24:9 (cf. Deut. 24:7,10-13,17)

24:13-17 This is another list of the acts of evil people who God apparently ignores.

- they rebel against God's way, Job 24:13

- they murder and steal from the poor and helpless, Job 24:14

- they commit adultery, Job 24:15 (they think God does not or will not see and respond!)

- they break into homes and businesses by night and flee the light of day, Job 24:16
(again, God does not respond, Job 24:17)

Where is the God of Justice? Where is the reality of "the two ways"
(cf. Leviticus 26; Deut. 30:15,19; Psalm 1). God's inactivity mocks God's word and promises!

24:13 "those who rebel"
This is a Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE (BDB 597, KB 632). It denotes
those who openly and flagrantly flaunt God's ways (cf. Num. 14:9; Jos. 22:16,18,19;
Ezek. 2:3; 20:38; Dan. 9:5,9). Only here in Job is it used of rebellion against "light"
(which is an idiom for Deity). This is open-eyed disregard for God and His ways (cf. Job 24:13b,c)!

▣ "ways. . .paths"
These are in a synonymous parallel relationship. A godly life was viewed
as a clear, straight, unobstructed path. There are numerous allusions to
this imagery in the OT (i.e., Ps. 25:4; 27:11; 86:11; 119:35,105; Isa.
40:14).

God's way is not hidden from His people but is clearly revealed (i.e.,
Mosaic covenant). Our daily task is to walk in it and bring honor to
Him. How much of God's revelation was available to Edomites (or for that
matter, Salemites, cf. Genesis 14; Ninevites, cf. Jonah) is uncertain.

verses.zh: 杀人的黎明起来，杀害困苦穷乏人，夜间又作盗贼。
verses.en: Before daybreak[NOTE:1] the murderer rises up;he kills the poor and the needy;in the night he is[NOTE:2] like a thief.[NOTE:3]
notes: The text simply has לָאוֹר (laʾor, “at light” or “at daylight”), probably meaning just at the time of dawn.
In a few cases the jussive is used without any real sense of the jussive being present (see GKC 323 §109.k).
The point is that he is like a thief in that he works during the night, just before the daylight, when the advantage is all his and the victim is most vulnerable.
verses.commentary:
24:14-15 These two verses could be literal or figurative. They
address the problem of humans treating other humans as objects for
personal gratification or aggrandizement! God loves people! People are
the only permanent aspect of this creation.
God's ways are meant to benefit all humans!

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

verses.zh: 奸夫等候黄昏，说：必无眼能见我，就把脸蒙蔽。
verses.en: And the eye of the adulterer watches for the twilight,thinking,[NOTE:1] ‘No eye can see me,’and covers his face with a mask.
notes: Heb “saying.”

verses.zh: 盗贼黑夜挖窟窿；白日躲藏，并不认识光明。
verses.en: In the dark the robber[NOTE:1] breaks into houses,[NOTE:2] but by day they shut themselves in;[NOTE:3] they do not know the light.[NOTE:4]
notes: The phrase “the robber” has been supplied in the English translation for clarification.
This is not the idea of the adulterer, but of the thief. So some commentators reverse the order and put this verse after v. 14.

The verb חִתְּמוּ (khittemu) is the Piel from the verb חָתַם (khatam, “to seal”). The verb is now in the plural, covering all the groups mentioned that work under the cover of darkness. The suggestion that they “seal,” i.e., “mark” the house they will rob, goes against the meaning of the word “seal.”
Some commentators join this very short colon to the beginning of v. 17: “they do not know the light. For together…” becomes “for together they have not known the light.”
verses.commentary:
24:16 "They do not know the light"
This is imagery. Evil people act in secrecy/darkness to conceal their
selfish acts (cf. John 3:19-21). The word "light" (BDB 21) is
used three times in this paragraph (Job 24:13,14,16). Obviously in Job 24:13
it refers to God, which is the thrust of Job 24:16c.

It is used literally in Job 24:14 for "the dawn" (another word
for the same time period is used in Job 24:17a).

verses.zh: 他们看早晨如幽暗，因为他们晓得幽暗的惊骇。
verses.en: For all of them,[NOTE:1] the morning is to them like deep darkness;they are friends with the terrors of darkness.
notes: Heb “together.”
verses.commentary:
24:17 "For the morning is the same to him as thick darkness" This
verse seems to refer to God's complete knowledge of all things. It is connected to
Job 24:13,16c, which is a reference to God as "the light." Evil seeks
darkness, Job 24:14,15,16a,b, but God knows (cf. Ps. 139:11-12).

The implication is that the God who knows (opposite of Job 24:14a,b)
will eventually bring the evil ones to justice (i.e., Job 24:18-20).

verses.zh: 这些恶人犹如浮萍快快飘去。他们所得的分在世上被咒诅；他们不得再走葡萄园的路。
verses.en: [NOTE:1] You say,[NOTE:2] ‘He is foam[NOTE:3] on the face of the waters;[NOTE:4] their portion of the land is cursedso that no one goes to their vineyard.[NOTE:5]
notes: Many commentators find vv. 18-24 difficult on the lips of Job, and so identify this unit as a misplaced part of the speech of Zophar. They describe the enormities of the wicked. But a case can also be made for retaining it in this section. Gordis thinks it could be taken as a quotation by Job of his friends’ ideas.
The verb “say” is not in the text; it is supplied here to indicate that this is a different section.
Or “is swift.”
The wicked person is described here as a spray or foam upon the waters, built up in the agitation of the waters but dying away swiftly.

The text reads, “he does not turn by the way of the vineyards.” This means that since the land is cursed, he/one does not go there. Bickell emended “the way of the vineyards” to “the treader of the vineyard” (see RSV, NRSV). This would mean that “no wine-presser would turn towards” their vineyards.
verses.commentary:
24:18-25 The last cycle of Job's three comforters' speeches and Job's
response is not complete. The reasons for this are uncertain.

- they give up because they cannot get Job to admit his sin

- the MT has been damaged in transmission

Many scholars see Job 24:18-25 as part of #2. These verses seem more
appropriate for Job's three comforters than Job himself. It is not that
Job denies "the two ways," he just asserts it does not fit his
situation.

It is difficult to follow the imagery of this paragraph. It is also
difficult to identify the acts of the evil humans and the acts of God.

- "they," "their," "them" – Job 24:18,23,24

- "he" (i.e., God) – Job 24:21-23

The JPSOA has a footnote at Job 24:18-25 which says, "From here to
the end of the chapter the translation is largely conjectural."
This paragraph is difficult to translate and comprehend.

verses.zh: 干旱炎热消没雪水；阴间也如此消没犯罪之辈。
verses.en: The drought[NOTE:1] as well as the heatsnatch up the melted snow;[NOTE:2] so the grave[NOTE:3] snatches up the sinner.[NOTE:4]
notes: Or “dryness.” The term צִיָּה (tsiyyah) normally refers to a dry region, a wilderness or desert. Here the focus is on dryness.
Heb “the waters of the snow.”
Or “Sheol.”

Heb “The grave [] they have sinned.” The verb “snatch up/away” is understood by parallelism. If the perfect verb is maintained, the line also implies the relative pronoun, “the grave [snatches] [those who] have sinned.” If the verb is emended from the perfect to a participle by deleting or moving the ו (vav) from חטאו to חוטא, it reads “the grave [snatches] one who sins.”
verses.commentary:
24:19 "Sheol" See

SPECIAL TOPIC: SHEOL, I. B.

As heat takes away snow, so Sheol takes away sinners. Job 24:19
implies they die quickly; Job 24:20 implies they are forgotten in death.

verses.zh: 怀他的母（原文是胎）要忘记他；虫子要吃他，觉得甘甜；他不再被人记念。不义的人必如树折断。
verses.en: The womb[NOTE:1] forgets him, the worm feasts on him,no longer will he be remembered.Like a tree, wickedness will be broken down.
notes: Here “womb” is synecdoche, representing one’s mother.

verses.zh: 他恶待（或译：他吞灭）不怀孕不生养的妇人，不善待寡妇。
verses.en: He preys on[NOTE:1] the barren and childless woman[NOTE:2] and does not treat the widow well.
notes: The form in the text is the active participle, “feed; graze; shepherd.” The idea of “prey” is not natural to it. R. Gordis (Job, 270) argues that third he (ה) verbs are often by-forms of geminate verbs, and so the meaning here is more akin to רָעַע (raʿaʿ, “to crush”). The LXX seems to have read something like הֵרַע (heraʿ, “oppressed”).
Heb “the childless [woman], she does not give birth.” The verbal clause is intended to serve as a modifier here for the woman. See on subordinate verbal clauses GKC 490 §156.d, f.
verses.commentary:
24:21-22 The interpretive question is, "does the 'he' refer to God or
'the affluent sinner'"?

- God – NASB (hard to tell with capitalized "He's"), NKJV, RSV, TEV

- wealthy, powerful sinner – LXX, Peshitta, Rotherham's Emphasized Bible

- mixed – JPSOA (mostly sinner), REB, NET Bible

Is Job claiming not only God's indifference (Job 24:12c) but also His
active help for the wicked (Job 24:23)? It seems so. The unfairness of
life is a major theological issue for Job. Is God the God of justice?

It seems to me that Job 24:21 and 22 refer to the powerful, wealthy
sinner ("he" does not refer to God) but Job 24:23 refers to God
("he" does refer to Deity, cf. Job 12:6).

verses.zh: 然而　神用能力保全有势力的人；那性命难保的人仍然兴起。
verses.en: But God[NOTE:1] drags off the mighty by his power;when God[NOTE:2] rises up against him, he has no faith in his life.[NOTE:3]
notes: God has to be the subject of this clause. None is stated in the Hebrew text, but “God” has been supplied in the translation for clarity.
Heb “he”; the referent (God) has been specified in the translation for clarity. See the note on the word “life” at the end of the line.

This line has been given a number of interpretations due to its cryptic form. The verb יָקוּם (yaqum) means “he rises up.” It probably is meant to have God as the subject, and be subordinated as a temporal clause to what follows. The words “against him” are not in the Hebrew text, but have been supplied in the translation to specify the object and indicate that “rise up” is meant in a hostile sense. The following verb וְלֹא־יַאֲמִין (veloʾ yaʾamin), by its very meaning of “and he does not believe,” cannot have God as the subject, but must refer to the wicked.

verses.zh: 神使他们安稳，他们就有所倚靠；　神的眼目也看顾他们的道路。
verses.en: God[NOTE:1] may let them rest in a feeling of security,[NOTE:2] but he is constantly watching[NOTE:3] all their ways.[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “he”; the referent (God) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
The expression לָבֶטַח (lavetakh, “in security”) precedes the verb that it qualifies—God “allows him to take root in security.” For the meaning of the verb, see Job 8:15.
Heb “his eyes are on.”
The meaning of the verse is that God may allow the wicked to rest in comfort and security, but all the time he is watching them closely with the idea of bringing judgment on them.

verses.zh: 他们被高举，不过片时就没有了；他们降为卑，被除灭，与众人一样，又如谷穗被割。
verses.en: They are exalted for a little while, and then they are gone;[NOTE:1] they are brought low[NOTE:2] like all others and gathered in,[NOTE:3] and like a head of grain they are cut off.’[NOTE:4]
notes: The Hebrew throughout this section (vv. 18-24) interchanges the singular and the plural. Here again we have “they are exalted…but he is not.” The verse is clear nonetheless: the wicked rise high, and then suddenly they are gone.

The verb is the Hophal of the rare verb מָכַךְ (makhakh), which seems to mean “to bend; to collapse.” The text would read “they are made to collapse like all others.” There is no reason here to change “like others” just because the MT is banal. But many do, following the LXX with “like mallows.” The LXX was making a translation according to sense. R. Gordis (Job, 271) prefers “like grass.”

The verb קָפַץ (qafats) actually means “to shut in,” which does not provide exactly the idea of being gathered, not directly at least. But a change to קָטַף (qataf, “pluck”) while attractive, is not necessary.
This marks the end of the disputed section, taken here to be a quotation by Job of their sentiments.
verses.commentary:
24:24 The wicked may prosper for a season but in time they will
reap what they have sown (cf. Psalm 73)! This is a
statement of the rigid validity of "the two ways" that Job has
several times rejected!

notes: The word אַל (ʾal, “not”) is used here substantivally (“nothing”).
verses.commentary:
24:25 Job emphatically says
"show me if I am incorrect"! Life is unfair. The wicked do
prosper. The righteous do suffer. Where is the God of promise and
justice? He seems not to care (cf. Job 24:12c). This is the theological
issue of the book of Job!

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which
means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the
light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not
relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare
your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is
the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every
paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

- In Job 23, Job again asks to go to court and lay out his case for vindication before God.

- In Job 24, Job accuses God of failing to hold court (i.e., "times," Job 24:1a).

- Many scholars (see notes in Oxford Annotation Bible, NRSV, p. 651) have questioned
if Job 24:18-25 reflects Job's thoughts.

- Some attribute them to one of the three comforters. The RSV and NET Bible add
"you say" to Job 24:18.

- NJB completely reorders several chapters in Job to try to fix he broken cycle
of the three comforters and Job's response to each (see chart of the dialogues in
Contextual Insights, chapter 20).

- Some think it was added by a later traditional Jewish scribe to make Job more
orthodox (NIDOTTE, vol. 1, p. 239; vol. 2, p. 629).

- NIDOTTE, vol. 2, p. 629, suggests Job 24:18-24 is a series of imprecations
spoken by Job against the wicked.
